title: Disciplinary Knowledge Isn’t the Same in Every Subject
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart continues his series on disciplinary knowledge by testing whether one definition fits every school subject. Using Learning First's classification of subjects as single-discipline, multi-discipline or practical, he proposes a progression from substantive knowledge to substantive concepts, then disciplinary knowledge, then disciplinary concepts. In history, geography and science the later stages are about how we know, built up from small concrete cases such as sources, fieldwork or experiments. In music, design and technology, PE and computing the cases instead show what good looks like, so he argues the definition should be widened to cover what counts as doing the work well. English and RE draw on more than one field at once, while maths and languages put fluency first and fit the framework poorly. His conclusion is that disciplinary concepts are what many cases add up to, not vocabulary handed over first, and that a knowledge-rich curriculum is connected rather than a list of disconnected facts.
points: Disciplinary knowledge is usually defined as how a subject establishes, tests and revises what it knows, but that definition fits history, geography and science far better than practical subjects.
For music, design and technology, PE and computing the author proposes widening the definition to include what counts as doing the work well, with concepts of quality forming from exemplars.
Disciplinary concepts such as evidence, change or quality should emerge from accumulated concrete cases rather than being taught as vocabulary before students have met any of the knowing behind them.
Subjects like English and RE need the curriculum to say which field is being taught, since the answer to how do we know differs between, for example, a theologian, a sociologist and a philosopher.
Maths and languages put fluency first and reach their discipline later, so the same template should not be forced on every subject.
quotes: Disciplinary knowledge is commonly understood as how the subject establishes, tests and revises what it knows but that definition suits some subjects better than others.
Take two students who both know that the Romans built roads. One knows it as an isolated fact. The other connects it to trade, the army and control, and is beginning to build a schema.

Science also shows the risk of a disciplinary component reduced to procedure. Working scientifically can become fair tests, variables and write ups, divorced from how scientists came to believe what they believe.
I argue that the progression of conceptual development necessarily changes, not in structure but in focus.

If the definition covers only how claims are tested, it describes history well and these subjects badly. For these subjects, I’d widen the definition: disciplinary knowledge is how a field establishes, tests and revises what it knows and, where the field is one of practice, what counts as doing it well.
Learning First is blunt that students cannot realistically attempt mathematical proof, and that the disciplinary framework fits maths poorly.

In every case the concepts are what the cases add up to, not vocabulary handed over first. That is also the answer to the claim that a knowledge rich curriculum is a list of disconnected facts: the knowledge is connected and the connections are the point.
